  8.2       SI units
The system of units used in engineering and science
is the Système Internationale d’Unités (International         Some derived units are given special names. For exam-
System of Units), usually abbreviated to SI units, and is     ple, force = mass × acceleration has units of kilogram
based on the metric system. This was introduced in 1960       metre per second squared, which uses three of the base
and has now been adopted by the majority of countries         units, i.e. kilograms, metres and seconds. The unit of kg
as the official system of measurement.                        m/s2 is given the special name of a Newton.
The basic seven units used in the SI system are listed in     Table 8.2 contains a list of some quantities and their
Table 8.1 with their symbols.                                 units that are common in engineering.
There are, of course, many units other than these seven.
These other units are called derived units and are             8.3    Common prefixes
defined in terms of the standard units listed in the table.
For example, speed is measured in metres per second,          SI units may be made larger or smaller by using prefixes
therefore using two of the standard units, i.e. length and    which denote multiplication or division by a particular
time.                                                         amount.

An angle is the amount of rotation between two straight
lines. Angles may be measured either in degrees or in
radians.

  27.1         Introduction
The volume of any solid is a measure of the space occu-
pied by the solid. Volume is measured in cubic units
such as mm3 , cm3 and m3 .                                           h                                 l
   This chapter deals with ﬁnding volumes of common
solids; in engineering it is often important to be able to
                                                                                b
calculate volume or capacity to estimate, say, the amount
of liquid, such as water, oil or petrol, in different shaped   Figure 27.1
containers.

prisms (called cuboids), triangular prisms and circular

prisms (called cylinders).
